entry.title: Three stack bugs in the original, found by proving rewrites
entry.summary: A production batch of six task-system functions yielded four verified rewrites and two partial proofs, and the two partial proofs are the interesting part: in three of the six functions the original code itself cleans up the stack wrongly after some calls, so those paths return into garbage and crash. The proofs had to be split into completing paths, which pass, and faulting paths, which are demonstrated crashing.
entry.content:
A production batch of six task-system functions yielded four verified rewrites and two partial proofs, and the two partial proofs are the interesting part: in three of the six functions the original code itself cleans up the stack wrongly after some calls, so those paths return into garbage and crash. The proofs had to be split into completing paths, which pass, and faulting paths, which are demonstrated crashing.

What was asked

Rewrite six neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original on the checker, with at least a thousand trials and a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

  • Verified Four functions proved fully: two task initialisers, one virtual route-following step with lazy global caches and a double-precision helper call, and one accept-or-reject check with two virtual calls.
  • Verified In three functions the original mis-cleans the stack on some paths: one never cleans a three-word call (its flag and out-word are then read back from never-written slots, so they are always stale), one pops four bytes too many per report call and per marker trio, and one pops twelve too many around its script block. Each faulting path was run and observed crashing; no completing rewrite can match a crashing original, so these are recorded as passing stages plus fault demonstrations.
  • Verified Three functions read a never-written aligned-frame scratch slot into an output word. Under the checker's zero stack fill that word is zero, which is what the rewrites store; each proof documents it.
  • Inferred The faulting paths look like dead or defensive code, or paths the game's own state never reaches: each smells like a caller/callee declaration mismatch, and each crashes in the real game too, since no callee behaviour can balance the arithmetic.

What was decided or recommended

The two affected functions are recorded as partly proven: the completing-paths stage passes on the stock checker with mutants caught, and a retry kit (full rewrite, stage contract and verdict, fault analysis, fault-demonstration contract) waits in the lane folder. The next lane should read the fault analysis first and decide between accepting the stage and attempting fault parity, which is expected to be fragile. A reusable lesson: when the original faults on some trials, check the caller's own stack arithmetic before suspecting the contract — the bytes of one cleanup instruction settled two of these cases.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's stage contracts for the two affected functions (all completing paths pass), then run the retry folder's full contracts, which steer trials into the faulting paths and show the original faulting where the rewrite completes. The lane log and report name every file.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two self-inflicted faults cost the most time. First, a wrong nibble in a contract's function field sent a run at the wrong bytes; the contract linter catches this in a second and should run before every first attempt. Second, pin phases that looked independent combined to make a callee path unsatisfiable, producing a vacuous verdict; aligning one pin to odd trials fixed it. A transient build lock from a stale handle was fixed by removing the built file after confirming no process held it.

entry.title: Production lane: 28 text-field functions verified, two held by a global-fill gap
entry.summary: A production batch of 30 small input-ui functions finished with 28 verified on the stock checker and two deferred: scripted values for game globals demonstrably failed to reach those two functions' reads, while the checker's own control contracts pass, so the rewrites are kept for a later re-run.
entry.content:
A production batch of 30 small input-ui functions finished with 28 verified on the stock checker and two deferred: scripted values for game globals demonstrably failed to reach those two functions' reads, while the checker's own control contracts pass, so the rewrites are kept for a later re-run.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of 30 neighbouring text-field functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the project checker, one contract per function, each with a deliberately wrong version that must fail.

What was found

  • Verified 28 of 30 functions pass 1,200 trials each with a caught wrong version, covering child selection, key classifiers, cursor and mode handling, virtual-call forwarding, float scaling and validation, and a five-record text builder.
  • Verified Eleven functions return through byte-only writes that preserve the upper 24 bits of the last value in the register. Small test inputs hide this; only values above one byte catch it.
  • Verified One builder function leaks its call windows on purpose and its finalizer pops thirteen words. A probe with the wrong pop size faults exactly as predicted; with the right size it completes balanced.
  • Verified A computed tail jump through a virtual table verifies with a normal stub. A no-cleanup stub models the wrong callee shape and fails the stack-pointer check.
  • Verified Two functions could not be steered: the values scripted for the game globals they read never took effect (pinned and random fills alike), while the checker's own global-read controls pass on the same worker. Their rewrites and contracts are kept for a re-run.
  • Verified A suspected calling-convention bug in one function turned out to be the lane's own arithmetic slip. A probe showing clean completion forced a recount before anything was reported.

What was decided or recommended

Ship the 28 verified rewrites. Re-run the two deferred functions once scripted global values reach reads; their contracts need no changes. Any lane whose wrong version passes on a function that reads game globals should check whether its fills actually land before trusting the proof.

How to reproduce it

Each function has a contract and a verdict file in the lane scratch folder; the generators, table-extraction scripts and the probes (including the global-fill controls) sit beside them. The two deferred functions reproduce as a passing correct run with a passing wrong version, and a vacuous verdict with unfired callees, respectively.

What was confusing or went wrong

The global-fill gap cost the most time: every link in the chain (driver request bytes, worker source order, setup parsing, relocations) reads correctly, the controls pass, yet the two functions behave as pristine. The root cause is still unknown. Separately, one mutant passed sixty trials because the callee script cycled the identical sequence as the stack input; offsetting one of them caught it at once.

entry.title: Naming 150 shader, targeting and task functions
entry.summary: Named 147 of 150 consecutive game functions covering a vehicle paint shader effect, the ped targeting object, navmesh route-following tasks, vehicle enter and exit tasks, and a set of placeholder task constructors.
entry.content:
Named 147 of 150 consecutive game functions covering a vehicle paint shader effect, the ped targeting object, navmesh route-following tasks, vehicle enter and exit tasks, and a set of placeholder task constructors.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name with confidence for each function in the batch, working out what each group does first, using strings, imports, known callers, class tables and verified rewrites as evidence.

What was found

Verified Joining over a thousand earlier naming proposals with the symbol table recovers the task vtable protocol: clone, task id, make abortable, create first and next sub task, and control sub task sit in fixed slots across the whole task family.

Verified Six targeting methods were named directly from verified rewrite documents, and nine placeholder task constructors were identified by reading the class tables each one installs.

Inferred The vehicle enter and exit tasks run a status machine: each class has a jump table mapping status numbers to readable names, a counter that advances the status, a setter for it, and a builder that creates the sub task for the current status.

Inferred Vtable slots with the same number can mean different things in different class families: the slot that selects a sub task id in combat tasks holds the whole sub task builder in vehicle tasks. Behaviour, not slot number, decided those names.

What was decided or recommended

Follow the recovered slot protocol for future task batches, but verify giant overrides against the constructors they call before trusting the slot. Reading a class table from the image settles constructor identity and exposes stubbed slots a sibling class never overrode.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the mapped image, resolve callees against the merged symbols, prior lane names and verified rewrite index, collect referenced strings and constants, read the class tables for constructor and slot attribution, then name from the strongest signal per function.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two shell commands failed on quoting before all dumping moved into scripts. One assumed slot transfer was wrong: the sibling shader class leaves the slot a stub, so the name came from the function's own behaviour instead.

entry.title: Lifting the input-ui holders: ten free functions, four shapes
entry.summary: What was asked: lift the 35 verified routines sharing the input-ui name prefix, a group chosen by name rather than by class, and find what data they actually share. (Verified: all 35 rewrites triaged by signature, doc comment and global/callee use.)
entry.content:
What was asked: lift the 35 verified routines sharing the input-ui name prefix, a group chosen by name rather than by class, and find what data they actually share. (Verified: all 35 rewrites triaged by signature, doc comment and global/callee use.)

What was found: the prefix is a pipeline, not a structure. The 35 routines span about twenty data shapes. The largest real shape is the element holder family: every holder opens with a table pointer and an id word whose low bits are stamped from a global counter and whose middle bits are folded from two polled answers. Three constructor routines proved to be byte-identical instances of one routine by diff. A sibling verified batch names the family as a generic callback-holder template with verified constructors, copy constructors and teardown, which are the natural next lift. (Verified: file diffs; sibling file headers.)

What was decided: lift the holder family (six routines as four methods on one owning type), plus the state-record copy, the bounds accumulator, the float predicate and the entry scanner: ten routines proven against their rewrites with 24,591 differential comparisons and eleven deliberately wrong versions caught, with 36 host tests. Small unrelated shapes were kept in separate modules rather than merged into a drawer. The remaining 25 routines were ranked by outside-call count for the next lane; the mode-table pair and the state initialiser are the easiest next proofs. (Verified: test runs on the 32-bit target and the 64-bit host.)

Method notes for the next free-function group: hash neighbour bodies before lifting once; run the differential suite in release mode when a rewrite relies on wrapping arithmetic; compare float-carrying logs bit for bit because NaN never equals itself; and plant virtual slots as real tables pointing at recording stubs. Full detail is in the lane report.

entry.title: Naming combat, cover and effects functions: slot 24 selects the subtask id
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions were named 117 ways, and the main result is a new virtual-slot meaning: slot 24 on combat subtasks picks which subtask to build next by type id, pairing with the subtask factory at slot 25 found earlier.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions were named 117 ways, and the main result is a new virtual-slot meaning: slot 24 on combat subtasks picks which subtask to build next by type id, pairing with the subtask factory at slot 25 found earlier.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of consecutive unnamed game functions, mostly combat-ai and cover tasks with some effects code at the end, working from strings, called functions, virtual-table slots and prior lane names.

What was found

Verified Slot 24 on every combat subtask returns a task type id, from constant ids for charge and execute subtasks to weapon-state and decision-maker queries for fire and retreat subtasks.

Verified Slot 22 has no single meaning even inside one family: sibling overrides abort, retarget, swap aim nodes or relink posture nodes, and the cover family uses a different argument count, so each override needed its own name.

Verified Four functions the inventory listed as unreferenced were placed into their virtual tables by scanning read-only data for pointers to them, which also confirmed their classes through type records.

Verified Twenty-one task type ids were read from constant stubs, and a sweep of every such stub in the binary resolved several more referenced ids while leaving six still unidentified.

What was decided or recommended

Slot 24 is called select subtask id and slot 22 is named per function. The type-id getter keeps the newest lanes spelling until the project picks one of the two spellings in use. The next lane should map the effects data sections to their lookup tables, identify six unknown task ids, and run the pointer scan on every batch since inventory tags miss entries.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped executable image, never the raw file at a mapped address. Decode one known constant stub first to confirm the mapping, gather per-function evidence of calls, strings and constants into one table, cross virtual slots against prior lane names, and scan read-only data for pointers to anything apparently unreferenced before leaving it unnamed.

What was confusing or went wrong

A redirected output file came out in an encoding that read back garbled, so later reads used the structured evidence file instead. Two commands ran slowly under load but delivered complete results. The two competing spellings of the type-id getter took a three-way check that settled nothing, and time ran out on the collision-dispatch family and the effects table mapping, which were documented rather than guessed.

entry.title: Running the skipped pointers that could not be read
entry.summary: Asked: 377 verified functions had a call whose pointer argument the proof skips and whose buffer nobody could read. A reading lane had studied every skipped pointer in the original code and left these undecided. We ran them with the buffer compared instead: a snapshot of the words behind each skipped pointer at each call, 300 trials on the stock checker, then narrowing and per-site reruns for everything that failed.
entry.content:
Asked: 377 verified functions had a call whose pointer argument the proof skips and whose buffer nobody could read. A reading lane had studied every skipped pointer in the original code and left these undecided. We ran them with the buffer compared instead: a snapshot of the words behind each skipped pointer at each call, 300 trials on the stock checker, then narrowing and per-site reruns for everything that failed.

Found: 238 functions settled without repair. In 69 the rewrite hands over the same words. In 120 the buffer is uninitialised at the call, so there is nothing stored to compare. In 49 the words differ but the callee writes before it reads or never touches the buffer, so the earlier proof stands. One function was wrong and is repaired and re-proved: a wrapper that dropped its entry register and passed zero where the original passes a pointer the nested converter reads through. 22 more functions show the same shape, stored words differing where the callee reads first, and are specified for repair. The rest are deferred with reasons: sites that cannot be snapshotted, callees in the encrypted region, diffs that stay hidden, and a cluster that diverges only in termination with or without snapshots, which lives in the base proof rather than the buffer.

Decided: running settles what reading could not, and two rerun tricks do most of it. Rerunning with a zero stack fill turns every uninitialised word into a match, so any remaining diff is stored. The patterned fill is exactly invertible, so pattern reruns classify words by arithmetic. Both were validated against controls. The repair backlog is ordered by callee verdict: read-first sites first.

Reproduce: the lane folder holds the list, all run verdicts, the consolidation script, and the per-function results; the one repair ships with its contract, verdict and caught mutant.

entry.title: Production batch: three fire-task dispatches verified, plus a driver output trap
entry.summary: Three neighbouring fire-task dispatch routines (about one thousand bytes each) were rewritten in Rust and verified against the originals with twelve hundred trials each, including fault-parity and wrong-version runs. The batch also exposed a tooling trap worth knowing: the checker driver writes its run summary to results.json next to itself, which silently overwrote this lane's deliverable of the same name twice.
entry.content:
Three neighbouring fire-task dispatch routines (about one thousand bytes each) were rewritten in Rust and verified against the originals with twelve hundred trials each, including fault-parity and wrong-version runs. The batch also exposed a tooling trap worth knowing: the checker driver writes its run summary to results.json next to itself, which silently overwrote this lane's deliverable of the same name twice.

What was asked

Rewrite three medium-sized routines from the same task-dispatch module and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original, with contracts that script every outgoing call (including calls into the encrypted first megabyte of code and calls through object function tables) and a deliberately wrong version per routine that must fail.

What was found

  • Verified All three routines verified on the stock checker with no deferrals: one over four staged contracts (including fault-parity trials for a re-initialisation path), one over three stages, one in a single contract. Every wrong version failed on exactly the word it changed.
  • Verified The driver summary clobber is real and repeatable: each run replaced the lane's results file with run statistics. Both losses were reconstructed from the per-contract verdict files. Redirecting driver output to a subdirectory avoids it.
  • Verified The float gates in this family are equality tests, not NaN tests. A compare-against-zero followed by a parity-tested flag check branches exactly when the value is not positive zero (any nonzero value or NaN takes the same side). A direct equality comparison in the rewrite matches bit-exactly.
  • Verified Direct calls into the encrypted region intercept and script normally, confirming earlier lanes; no routine here needed deferring for that reason.

What was decided or recommended

  • Consider renaming the driver's summary output so it cannot collide with lane deliverables, or briefing lanes to redirect driver output. Until then, a running lane's results file should not be read as authoritative mid-run.
  • Lanes modelling flag-based float branches should work out the parity logic from the flag definitions rather than assuming a NaN test; the wrong first guess cost this lane one probe cycle.

How to reproduce it

Run any checker driver copy from a folder containing a file named results.json and observe it replaced after the run. For the float gate, compare the taken side across positive zero, negative zero, nonzero values, and NaN inputs against a plain equality comparison.

What was confusing or went wrong

Time perception without the clock: the lane estimated forty minutes more had passed than the machine showed, nearly stopping an hour early. Two stack-map computations mixed decimal and hexadecimal offsets and were corrected from snapshot diffs. One diagnostics script initially ignored a register-skip setting and reported phantom differences until fixed.

entry.title: A wrong rewrite passed, and the checker could not see it
entry.summary: A production lane proving small input-system functions found that the checker's comparison of changed global variables ignores where inside a declared range each change happened, so a rewrite that stores the right values at the wrong addresses still passes. Every contract in the lane was rewritten to declare globals one word at a time, which restores the check, and nothing in the checker itself was changed.
entry.content:
A production lane proving small input-system functions found that the checker's comparison of changed global variables ignores where inside a declared range each change happened, so a rewrite that stores the right values at the wrong addresses still passes. Every contract in the lane was rewritten to declare globals one word at a time, which restores the check, and nothing in the checker itself was changed.

What was asked

Rewrite forty small neighbouring functions in Rust and prove each one behaves identically to the original, with a deliberately wrong version per function to show the proof can tell right from wrong.

What was found

Verified Thirty-nine of the forty functions were proved, each over one thousand trials with its wrong version caught. The remaining one cannot be proved as a single contract for a documented checker limitation.

Verified One wrong version stored its result one table slot too low and passed. Reading the checker's comparison code showed why: changed heap and stack words are recorded with their exact offsets, but changed globals are recorded with only the start address of the declared range, so all values written anywhere inside one range compare as an unordered pile. A second experiment confirmed the check runs but is blind to position: a wrong constant at the right place failed, a right value at the wrong place passed.

Verified Declaring each global word as its own range fixes the proofs without touching the checker: the same slot-shifted wrong version then fails, naming the two word addresses. All contracts in the lane use this shape.

Verified Two smaller lessons from the same batch. Direct calls into the encrypted first megabyte of the program are intercepted at the call site and verify normally, so that flag alone is not a reason to defer a function. And three functions read a floating-point value from uninitialized caller stack space; under the checker's zero stack fill they deterministically read zero, which is what the rewrites store, with the limitation recorded on each proof.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep declaring globals one word per range in new contracts until the comparison records word offsets.
  • Consider re-running earlier proofs whose contracts declare multi-word globals ranges with two or more written words: those proofs cannot show which word got which value, and a slot-shifted wrong version is the test that tells.
  • Do not defer functions only because they call into the encrypted region; defer only what the checker cannot intercept.

How to reproduce it

Write a contract whose function stores two different values to two words of one declared globals range, with a wrong version that swaps the two stores. The wrong version passes. Split the range into one range per word and run again: the wrong version fails. The lane's report names the comparison routine and the contracts that demonstrate both outcomes.

What was confusing or went wrong

The passing wrong version first looked like a mistake in the new contract, and only a second, louder wrong version showed the contract was fine and the comparison was weak. Six other first attempts failed for a sillier reason: the lane wrote callee arguments in push order instead of call order, which the checker caught every time.

entry.title: Same-period contract cyclers can starve whole code regions
entry.summary: Verified A production lane verifying a large ped-task function found that three groups of check trials never ran, not because the paths were rare but because the contract's cycling value lists all shared one period and stayed phase-locked: the trials that reached a region never carried the values that region needed. Giving the cyclers coprime periods fixed it, and all fifty helper stand-ins then fired.
entry.content:
Verified A production lane verifying a large ped-task function found that three groups of check trials never ran, not because the paths were rare but because the contract's cycling value lists all shared one period and stayed phase-locked: the trials that reached a region never carried the values that region needed. Giving the cyclers coprime periods fixed it, and all fifty helper stand-ins then fired.

What was asked

Rewrite one large game function in Rust and prove it identical with the checker, covering every helper it calls.

What was found

Verified Per-trial cycling lists (helper answers, pinned heap words) advance in lock-step by trial number. Three locks were found by reading per-helper fire counts:

  • One helper shared a single answer list between its gate call and its loop calls, so the loop-exhaustion path and the poll-fail path could never co-occur. Splitting the two call sites across two helper entries with independent lists fixed it.
  • Three period-four cyclers (a bypass-flag pin, an aux pin, a null-or-pointer answer list) all put their active value on the same trials, so the bypass always skipped the aux path. Moving one pin's active slot fixed it.
  • Several period-two and period-three answer lists aligned with the conditions that reach them, hiding branches. Coprime periods (four, five, eight) made every combination occur.

Verified Two smaller traps in the same function: float answers delivered in a vector register must be read as plain 32-bit words (a float-typed read picks up unrelated floating-point-stack leftovers), and the original's frame keeps two words of floating-point control-word residue that later snapshots observe, so the rewrite seeds them.

What was decided or recommended

When two cycling lists must combine (a reach condition plus a branch value), give them different periods so the combination occurs by arithmetic rather than luck, and check per-helper fire counts before the full run. A helper with zero firings after hundreds of trials is a lock, not bad luck.

How to reproduce it

Run any multi-branch contract, read the per-helper fire counts in the verdict, and list which trial residues reach each region versus which residues each cycler needs. The lane's generator script and contract show the fixed periods.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first full run passed every trial yet stayed vacuous with three helpers unfired, which looked like rarity until the residues were written out. A later period change silently re-locked two other regions the same way, found the same way. Nothing about the failure pointed at periods; only the fire counts did.

entry.title: lifting the interface font string
entry.summary: 6 October 2026 — Lane l-cls13 lifted the user-interface string class that measures and draws one line of text in a font: 18 verified methods restated as ordinary Rust on one owning type, each proven against its verified 32-bit rewrite on the same generated inputs, comparing results, every written byte and every collaborator call in order, floats bit for bit, with a deliberately wrong lift caught for each. 13 differential tests and 21 host tests pass. Nothing here counts as checker-verified; the lifts are proven against verified rewrites only.
entry.content:
6 October 2026 — Lane l-cls13 lifted the user-interface string class that measures and draws one line of text in a font: 18 verified methods restated as ordinary Rust on one owning type, each proven against its verified 32-bit rewrite on the same generated inputs, comparing results, every written byte and every collaborator call in order, floats bit for bit, with a deliberately wrong lift caught for each. 13 differential tests and 21 host tests pass. Nothing here counts as checker-verified; the lifts are proven against verified rewrites only.

What was asked

Turn the family's verified 32-bit rewrites — raw addresses, numbered callee slots, globals — into a portable type that owns its data, with every behaviour-carrying method restated and proven, following the sibling clip module's world-trait pattern.

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
Object shapeLive layout words, six flag bytes, a 256-byte text buffer, one row descriptor per indexed slotThe lifted type owns all of it; rows are a vector of descriptors with their own text
Backend notify shapeOne four-word call shape shared by four settersOne trait method serves all four call sites
Style ruleDraw mode with an unstyled string forces style two, else the stored tagOne rule restated once, used by the emitter and the measure pass
Text resolutionScratch converter or shared cache, eight words either wayTwo world methods answering word arrays; addresses never cross the trait
Float answersHook answers arrive through float-stack returns, which quiet signalling NaNsThe proof fake reproduces the quieting as bit operations; the lift stays pure
Text setter proofIts copier is proven under a non-writing stubThe lift models the forced terminator only; the copy is the world's work
Operating-system callsNone in the familyNothing goes behind the platform traits

What was decided

Globals travel as method arguments (slot selector, interface mode bytes, scale triple, display extents, default float); the shared cache needs no handle because it is a single global object; the deleting destructor is left to Drop; the two tiny unverified methods are listed as missing and not written from their names. Verified: the differential proof compares every call in order with its arguments on both sides. Inferred: the four flag bytes no verified method reads are stored state whose role is unestablished. Unknown: nothing reached by a lifted method.

How to reproduce

From the lane scratch folder: host tests run in the scratch workspace, and the proof crate runs its three differential suites on the 32-bit Windows target while also building on the 64-bit host with all targets checked. The proof includes the tracked rewrite files by path and scripts every callee and slot answer.

entry.title: 6 October 2026 The one-byte answer channel leaves log residue in the high bytes
entry.summary: Asked: a staged rewrite exited through the shared epilogue after a callee with an al answer, and the exit value mismatch showed high bytes matching neither zero nor the previous call's answer. Both sides agreed with each other on every other channel.
entry.content:
Asked: a staged rewrite exited through the shared epilogue after a callee with an al answer, and the exit value mismatch showed high bytes matching neither zero nor the previous call's answer. Both sides agreed with each other on every other channel.

FactValueWhat it means
Stub code for the al channelmasks the low byte in over the live registerThe live register at that point holds the call-log slot pointer, not the entry value: high bytes are log residue by construction (the source calls it residue semantics).
Log index resetper side, before each side's trialsBoth sides compute the same residue whenever they make the same calls in the same order, so the value is comparable.
Observed exit high bytesequal on both sides, nonzero, stable per trialConfirmed empirically: reading the full register after the call and returning it untouched passes; assuming zero or entry-preserved high bytes fails.

Decided: after an al callee, rewrites read the full 32-bit register and propagate it exactly like any scripted answer; the residue is part of the stub's deterministic answer, and under the real callee both sides would propagate its real high bytes the same way. Lane briefs should say this explicitly: never assume the high bytes are zero or preserved.

Reproduce: any contract where an exit value depends on full eax after an al call; compare returning the masked low byte against returning the full register. Verified on the stock worker.

Same session, second finding: image-base immediates passed as call arguments must go through the relocated-address helper, never as raw literals — the worker maps the image elsewhere and the comparison sees the relocated value. A mismatch that names only one register argument with otherwise identical logs is the signature.

entry.title: Naming the combat tasks: slot map, two new virtuals, and an RTTI trick
entry.summary: A batch of 150 consecutive combat-task functions yielded 138 names, and the fastest evidence was not reading code at all: crossing the class-lane vtable tables against descriptive names earlier lanes had already given resolves most virtual slots by majority vote.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 consecutive combat-task functions yielded 138 names, and the fastest evidence was not reading code at all: crossing the class-lane vtable tables against descriptive names earlier lanes had already given resolves most virtual slots by majority vote.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, mostly virtual methods of the combat AI task classes plus free helpers, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified Crossing per-class vtable slot tables against the merged lane names gives a slot-meaning map for complex tasks: slot 1 is clone, slot 3 returns the task type id, slot 5 is make-abortable, slot 6 is a float urgency, slots 15 to 17 find or set subtasks, and slots 18, 19 and 20 create the next subtask, create the first subtask, and control the subtask each tick, with dozens to hundreds of agreeing precedents each.

Verified Slots above 20 are family-specific, not global: slot 23 means one thing in the vehicle-driving task family and another in the combat-subtask family, so a slot name must never be copied across families unchecked.

Verified Two combat-subtask virtuals had no prior names. Slot 25 is a subtask factory dispatching on the task id argument: one override maps the exact id another class reports for itself to that class's constructor. Slot 23 queries the global combat decision maker for a response id, with one class overriding it by a constant.

Verified The combat task's slot 7 allocates an object whose runtime type record names it a flee dummy task, confirming the newest lane's create-dummy-task wording; its slot 6 returns the same urgency constant as an already-named urgency method on another class.

Inferred The free helpers around the methods form small clusters with readable roles: movement and weapon subtask factories, decision-maker range and factor queries, cover-slot search with a physics probe, group member selection, and one order-issuing routine built around a cover-me speech line.

What was decided or recommended

Named 138 of 150 functions and left 12 empty rather than guess: pure-math helpers with no calls, sweeps over unknown callee helpers, and bit-test predicates whose flag meanings are unknown. The next naming lane should identify the two unknown slot-array helpers and the class behind one heavily wrapped virtual call first, since several unnamed functions depend on them.

How to reproduce it

Build a script that loads the batch list, disassembles each function once from the mapped executable image, and records direct calls with their already-known names, string references, and cross-references from a single sweep of the code section. Resolve the virtual slots by joining the class-lane vtable data against the merged name lists before reading any single function. For factory-style methods, read the runtime type record behind any vtable the constructed object stamps: it names the created class directly.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three different wordings existed for the task-id getter across lane generations, and the oldest wording had the most votes; the newest lane's wording was followed instead, since naming conventions drift and recency wins ties. Several borrowed names for callees turned out to be placeholders or guesses from other lanes, so every reused name was treated as a hint until the code itself confirmed it.

entry.title: A constructor that returns to address zero, and a NaN trap in float compares
entry.summary: One function in this batch cannot be verified because the original always crashes on return: its epilogue pops two scratch words it zeroed itself and jumps to address zero, on every call. It has callers in the image, so this looks like a genuine defect in the original rather than dead code. A second function taught a subtler lesson: a float branch taken on below also fires on unordered, so NaN fails the test where a plain less-than would pass it.
entry.content:
One function in this batch cannot be verified because the original always crashes on return: its epilogue pops two scratch words it zeroed itself and jumps to address zero, on every call. It has callers in the image, so this looks like a genuine defect in the original rather than dead code. A second function taught a subtler lesson: a float branch taken on below also fires on unordered, so NaN fails the test where a plain less-than would pass it.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of 22 small input-ui functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the checker, one contract per function, each with its own deliberately wrong version.

What was found

Verified A 62-byte node constructor stores three arguments, calls a sub-object initialiser, then returns to address zero on all 1000 checker trials. It reserves eight bytes of stack scratch and never releases them, so its final pop and return consume the two zero words it stored, and execution continues at address zero. The image contains four direct callers of this function.

Verified A rectangle hit test over floats failed 145 of 1000 trials with a rewrite that used plain less-than for its four boundary checks. The original compares with a branch that is taken both on ordered-less and on unordered, so any NaN operand fails the test; the rewrite passed it. Writing the checks as negated greater-or-equal, which keeps NaN failing, made all 1000 trials pass with the wrong version still caught.

Verified The batch's three tree-search functions share one lower-bound walk with unsigned key compares, and the five csv token readers share one polling shape over two callees; per-call answer sequences with per-trial cycling cover every path including truncation, quoting, carriage-return skips and mid-loop end flags.

What was decided or recommended

The crashing constructor is recorded as deferred with reason other: no faithful rewrite can pass, because the original never completes and the checker's vacuity rule rightly refuses a verdict with zero clean original trials. The rewrite draft and contract are kept for the record. Future float rewrites should treat every conditional branch after a float compare as suspect until its unordered behaviour is checked against the branch type: below-or-equal keeps NaN, below fails it.

How to reproduce it

Run the batch contract for the node constructor: every trial ends with the original faulting at address zero while the rewrite returns normally, and the callee log shows the sub-object call fired once on each side, proving the crash happens after the call, on return. For the hit test, run any contract whose float inputs include NaN and compare a plain less-than rewrite against the original: the mismatches are exactly the trials where a NaN reaches a boundary check.

What was confusing or went wrong

The constructor crash first looked like a broken patch or a bad stub address, because the fault address was zero. Dropping the register comparison changed nothing, which ruled out the contract; only reading the epilogue word by word showed the stack imbalance. The hit-test failure first looked like a clamp error, and only the direction of the mismatch, the rewrite answering yes where the original answered no, pointed at the boundary branches and their unordered behaviour.

entry.title: A passing check that cannot see indirect calls
entry.summary: A production lane verified 39 of 40 small functions and found that the check meant to catch unintercepted calls does not fire when the unintercepted call goes through a register or object table.
entry.content:
A production lane verified 39 of 40 small functions and found that the check meant to catch unintercepted calls does not fire when the unintercepted call goes through a register or object table.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of 40 small neighbouring functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the project's differential checker, which intercepts outgoing calls and compares behaviour over a thousand trials.

What was found

Verified Thirty-nine functions passed at a thousand trials each, every one with its own deliberately wrong version that the contract caught. The group included object constructors, deleting destructors, callback trampolines and float helpers, several needing planted tables, scripted vector-register answers and snapshots of stack-built structures.

Verified One function could not be verified: it installs a fixed object table and then calls through it, so the target is real program code that no fabricated pointer can redirect. A short probe confirmed the original runs that code to completion and folds its answers into the result.

Verified In that probe the check for unintercepted calls passed with zero detections even though the original demonstrably made two of them. The check therefore sees unpatched direct calls only, not unpatched indirect ones. A passing result there is not proof that every outgoing call was intercepted.

What was decided or recommended

The unverifiable function was deferred with its draft rewrite and probe kept for a future checker that can observe native table calls. Lanes should confirm indirect-call coverage by reading every register and table call in the code, not from the check alone.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two call shapes looked impossible until a recount showed the return address had been left out of the stack arithmetic; both were then textbook. One wrong version passed because a second remainder operation erased the exact difference it introduced, so it was replaced with a genuinely different one. A shared code tail was first misread as returning a constant, and a pushed flag byte turned out to carry a status-flag image; probes caught both before the full runs.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's deferred-function probe contract for a few trials: stub only the first call, leave the two table calls unpatched, and observe the original completing with answers the stub never gave while the unintercepted-call check stays green. The probe files sit with the lane's deferred draft.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch: vehicle slots are shared, task slots are settled
entry.summary: 146 of 150 consecutive game functions got descriptive names, and the batch confirmed two reusable conventions: task vtable slots carry the same meaning across every task class, and several vehicle vtable slots point at one implementation shared by the helicopter, plane, car and bike tables.
entry.content:
146 of 150 consecutive game functions got descriptive names, and the batch confirmed two reusable conventions: task vtable slots carry the same meaning across every task class, and several vehicle vtable slots point at one implementation shared by the helicopter, plane, car and bike tables.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive project-style name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, with a confidence per name, working only from static evidence.

What was found

Verified Task slots are consistent across classes: slot 1 is clone, slot 5 is make-abortable, slot 17 is the per-frame ped update, complex-task slots 18/19/20 are create-next/create-first/control subtask, and the motion-task slots 26/27 are start/update behavior, each agreed by about a dozen sibling classes.

Verified Three vehicle slots (pose update, airborne check, wheel reset) resolve to a single shared implementation each, referenced from up to four vehicle class tables; the owning classes were identified by majority vote of neighbouring named slots.

Verified Five tiny neighbouring stat helpers are a millisecond time decomposition (days, hours, minutes, seconds, millis), confirmed by decoding their divide-by-constant magic numbers; nearby distance helpers convert with a miles-or-kilometres units switch.

Verified The materials manager's nine slots form a small name/index/entry lookup family with default fallback, and the batch also holds a complete stunt-jump subsystem (create, pool, save, load, per-frame update).

What was decided or recommended

Slot meaning is taken from cross-class agreement, never from one lane alone: where earlier lanes disagreed on three vehicle slots, the batch function's own callees broke the tie, and two single-lane votes look wrong and need a re-check. Four functions with unclear purpose were left unnamed rather than guessed.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table for the whole batch before naming anything: strings referenced, imports called, direct-call targets resolved against the merged name lists, every direct caller found by scanning the code section for call instructions, and every vtable reference found by scanning read-only data for pointers into the batch. Then read only the short functions and the ones the table leaves unclear.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Mapping a caller address to its function by nearest known start below misattributed one call site whose real enclosing function had no known start; every high-confidence name was therefore re-checked against vtable stamps, slot agreement or callee fingerprints instead of trusting caller labels alone.

Inferred Callees in the encrypted low code region disassemble as garbage statically, so the few names depending on them rest on call shape and sibling comparison; the checker sees them decrypted at run time.

entry.title: Three small traps from one input batch: dead stack reads, erased signedness, writes past the frame
entry.summary: Seventeen of eighteen small input-layer functions verified first try or after a short diagnosis; the three things that bit are all worth knowing before touching similar functions.
entry.content:
Seventeen of eighteen small input-layer functions verified first try or after a short diagnosis; the three things that bit are all worth knowing before touching similar functions.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of eighteen small neighbouring input-layer functions and prove each against the original with the checker, one contract and one deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified A function that reads an uninitialised stack word cannot be matched by reading your own stack slot: the compiler allocates a small slot with a push of a register, so the read returns the incoming register value, not the fill. The shipped rewrite stores the fill value with the proof explicitly limited to a uniform fill.

Verified A double modulo in one function provably erases signedness: reducing mod sixteen, subtracting from sixteen and reducing again gives the same result for signed and unsigned first reductions, so an unsigned-remainder mutant passed. Only the later signed division is observable, and its mutant fails. The rewrite documents which operation's signedness matters.

Verified Scripted callee writes past the end of a stack struct silently overwrite the return address and crash the original side with a zero instruction pointer. The fix is keeping every written word inside the real struct; a marker trace with distinctive words pinpoints each landing slot within minutes.

Verified Two smaller points: a zero-argument callee macro call needs a trailing comma to compile, and a thiscall callee's frame pointer is excluded from call comparison by giving it an empty register list while snapshots observe the pointed-to words.

What was decided or recommended

When a multi-call contract fails beyond the visible log prefix, trace with marker values before re-reading the code. When a function reads its own unwritten stack, prove the fill value and say so rather than mimicking the read. Deferred the one guard function whose conditional target is a large multi-call routine, for a large-function lane.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker: the residue function passes a thousand trials under a zero stack fill with the store-skipping mutant caught; the hook builder passes with fault parity on the null-allocator path and the unsigned-division mutant caught; the five-callee dispatch function passes with snapshots and downstream call arguments observing every live struct word.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three separate frame-address arithmetic slips on the five-callee function each looked like a checker defect in turn (a crash, a mystery value, a one-word mismatch) and each turned out to be my offset. The marker trace found all three. The unsigned-remainder mutant passing was briefly alarming until the residue-class argument showed it must pass.

entry.title: What the checker still could not do, and a candidate that can
entry.summary: A candidate seventh checker version now proves four shapes of function the stock checker had to defer: guards ending in a conditional jump to another routine, helpers taking a float on the float stack, call loops past the log cap, and vector registers of which only the low float matters. All four are proven by new self-test contracts, and the full existing suite gives identical verdicts.
entry.content:
A candidate seventh checker version now proves four shapes of function the stock checker had to defer: guards ending in a conditional jump to another routine, helpers taking a float on the float stack, call loops past the log cap, and vector registers of which only the low float matters. All four are proven by new self-test contracts, and the full existing suite gives identical verdicts.

What was asked

Give the checker the abilities whose absence is deferring functions: patching conditional tail jumps, observing float-stack call arguments, comparing call logs past the 1,024-call cap, narrowing a vector-register comparison to four bytes, and four reported defects. Each ability had to be an opt-in contract option that leaves every existing verdict unchanged.

What was found

Verified All four abilities are built, each with a passing rewrite, a caught wrong version, and a negative contract showing the option does the work. Ten new proof contracts run green, and 66 worker unit tests pass.

Verified Two reported defects were real and are fixed: an unknown return kind silently fell back to a 32-bit integer, and an unknown word-spec key silently resolved to random bits. Both now refuse the contract with a message, and none of the tracked contracts trip either refusal.

Verified Two deferred-function groups need no new ability. The computed tail jumps that pop the caller's word balance with the existing convention mechanism, and the vector-upper-byte case no longer reproduces on the current worker.

Inferred The remaining two defect reports could not be confirmed: no silent sequence-skew mechanism exists in the current worker, and out-of-range heap reads are a contract bug rather than a checker defect. Nothing was changed for either.

What was decided or recommended

The candidate is ready for coordinator review and install as a worker, driver, proofs and contracts change; the runtime crate rewrites build against is untouched. The recorded verdicts predate the current driver and should be re-recorded at install time. None of the deferred functions is one option away from passing: most lack any rewrite or contract, one needs re-contracting at its true location, and one is blocked by a separate one-bit float divergence.

How to reproduce it

Build the candidate worker and proofs from the lane's tree copy, run the ten proof contracts and confirm the battery script reports green, then run the tracked contracts with stock and candidate workers and confirm the pairwise comparison reports no differences.

What was confusing or went wrong

The digest's first accumulator slots collided with trampoline scratch space that looked free in the assignment list; the verdict detail shows only three calls, which hid the real failing call twice; and three lane verdicts turned out to run the wrong bytes through dropped address digits. Each is recorded in the lane report with the fix.

entry.title: Naming one hundred fifty NaturalMotion task functions
entry.summary: Verified A batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be the whole NaturalMotion ped-task system, and every one is now named: one hundred twenty at high confidence and thirty at medium, with none left blank.
entry.content:
Verified A batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be the whole NaturalMotion ped-task system, and every one is now named: one hundred twenty at high confidence and thirty at medium, with none left blank.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function from strings, imports, callers, class tables and behavior. No rewriting and no checker in this lane, only names with confidence levels.

What was found

Verified The group is the Euphoria task family: the NaturalMotion base task, its thirteen leaf behaviors such as balance, brace, flinch and shot, the blend-from-NM task, the complex NM task, and their shared helpers.

Verified The base task's per-frame method orchestrates the three behavior slots: the first run stops all behaviors and runs the start slot, later runs run the sustain slot and then the finish slot. This pins down what each slot means.

Verified Tasks request transitions by stamping a marker word holding the next task's id plus a stage byte, and a complex owner task was found testing that marker before creating its next sub-task.

Inferred The complex NM task's id getter returns a task id that was not in the id table, so it is a newly recorded id.

Verified Six constant-fill functions are default parameter rows for six behaviors, matched to their consumers by table base and row stride. Two widely called helpers turned out to be a plain memory comparison and the compiler's stack probe, not NM logic.

What was decided or recommended

  • Name the three behavior slots start, sustain and finish consistently across all leaves.
  • Name shared folded bodies once, noting every class whose table points at them.
  • Add the newly found complex NM task id to the task id table.
  • Correct the verified brace start-slot comment that calls it a per-frame update; it runs on first and retriggered processing.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the batch through the mapped executable image, validating the mapping by decoding one known id getter end to end. Collect callees, imports, referenced strings and constants per function, then scan the code section for direct callers of every batch member to name helpers by who calls them. Cross-check each table attribution against the per-class slot maps and read the verified rewrite notes of neighboring functions before theorizing about slot roles.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The caller counts from the decompiler-based inventory were wrong in at least three places: six initializers showed zero callers but each is called by an init loop, and a weapon helper showed one caller but has three. The function inventory also overruns one task update into its neighbor. Direct call scanning over the code section gave the true picture each time.

The two sustain slots resisted a clean distinction for a while because both build and send messages; what finally separated them was reading the base per-frame method and seeing it call one on the first run and the other afterwards.

entry.title: Two contract traps that let wrong rewrites pass, both caught by mutants
entry.summary: Verified A production batch of eighteen small memory-subsystem functions verified eighteen out of eighteen, and two of the eighteen only proved anything because each function got its own deliberately wrong version: in both cases the first wrong version passed every trial, showing the contract could not see the behaviour it claimed to check.
entry.content:
Verified A production batch of eighteen small memory-subsystem functions verified eighteen out of eighteen, and two of the eighteen only proved anything because each function got its own deliberately wrong version: in both cases the first wrong version passed every trial, showing the contract could not see the behaviour it claimed to check.

What was asked

Rewrite eighteen neighbouring game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical starting state over one thousand trials and compares return values, memory, stack, calls and faults. Every function also gets a wrong version that must fail.

What was found

Verified The first trap was a rotated pin pattern. One function reads a single grid cell chosen by two scripted indices, so the contract pinned thirty grid words to a shared six-value list rotated per cell. A wrong version using a different row stride passed all sixty probe trials. The shared list alternated zero and nonzero, so any two cells an even distance apart always agreed, and the stride difference was always even. Replacing the rotation with independent zero and nonzero streams per cell from a seeded random generator caught the wrong version within fifteen trials, and a second probe mutant confirmed the grid addresses were observed.

Verified The second trap was pristine-zero globals. One initialisation function writes zeros across two global ranges whose file bytes are already zero, so every write was invisible: a wrong version omitting one write passed all sixty trials. Random global fill plus a wrong version writing one instead of zero caught it within three trials.

Verified A third, smaller finding: one function flagged as calling into the encrypted first megabyte of code turned out to be checkable after all, because the call is a direct call the checker patches and scripts like any other. Nothing about the encrypted region was read or needed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Never pin a range of cells to rotations of one shared value list when a wrong address must be caught; give each cell an independent stream.
  • Always check what the pristine bytes hold before proving a function that writes constants; when they already hold the constant, fill randomly and make the wrong version write a different value.
  • Keep the per-function wrong version: both traps were invisible in the passing run and obvious the moment the wrong version passed.

How to reproduce it

Build any contract where the observable result depends only on whether a read word is zero, pin the candidate words to rotations of a zero-alternating list, and run a wrong version that reads a cell an even distance away: it passes. Replace the pins with seeded independent streams and rerun: it fails. For the globals trap, declare a range whose pristine bytes are zero, prove a zero-writing function, and run a wrong version that skips one write: it passes until the fill is randomised.

What was confusing or went wrong

The grid mutant passing sixty trials first looked like a correct proof of a wrong formula, which was briefly alarming. Reading the pin values trial by trial showed the parity alignment within minutes. The globals trap was found the same way: the passing wrong version was the signal, and checking the pristine bytes confirmed it. One further misread on a different function (a one-way copy mistaken for a swap, plus a wrong argument slot) failed loudly on the first run rather than passing quietly, which is the better failure mode.

entry.title: One configuration routine publishes uninitialized stack to a global
entry.summary: While verifying a batch of eight medium-sized routines, one of them turned out to read a stack slot it never stored and publish the block containing it to a global descriptor. The value is nondeterministic leftovers in the running game. The rewrite pins it to the harness's zero fill and notes the gap.
entry.content:
While verifying a batch of eight medium-sized routines, one of them turned out to read a stack slot it never stored and publish the block containing it to a global descriptor. The value is nondeterministic leftovers in the running game. The rewrite pins it to the harness's zero fill and notes the gap.

What was asked

Rewrite eight neighbouring routines in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the project checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares results, memory, calls and faults.

What was found

Verified All eight routines verified, one thousand trials each with no failures, and each with its own deliberately wrong version that the contract caught.

Verified In one routine's object-missing path, seven of eight descriptor words are stored and then all eight are written to the global. The eighth word is whatever the stack held at that moment. Both sides of the proof observe the harness's zero fill there, so the proof holds, but the game itself would publish a nondeterministic value.

Unknown Whether any consumer reads that word when the object is missing, which decides whether the quirk is benign or a real defect.

What was decided or recommended

The rewrite documents the pinned word and the proof records it as narrowed. A follow-up lane should read the consumer of that descriptor to settle the impact. Nothing about the checker needs to change: zero-filling uninitialized stack is already its documented behaviour for exactly this case.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the sink-configuration routine in the batch, take the path where its object global is null, and count the stored words against the eight published to the descriptor global. The project's lane report names the routine and the contract that pins the word.

What was confusing or went wrong

Three of my own mistakes were caught by the checker rather than by reading: a chain-walk condition with the branches backwards, a call result threaded from the wrong register, and a callee argument count off by one because a push sat three instructions above its call. The last one showed up as the original returning into a saved register value, which the register dump at the fault made obvious. Each took one fix and one re-run.

entry.title: Naming a run of task functions: slots, vtable readback and verified callers
entry.summary: All 150 functions in the batch were named, about half from vtable slot conventions and constructor shapes and the rest from disassembly with caller checks. The reliable signals were the virtual table slot, the vtable a constructor stores, and callers confirmed by byte search; strings and imports helped nowhere in this batch.
entry.content:
All 150 functions in the batch were named, about half from vtable slot conventions and constructor shapes and the rest from disassembly with caller checks. The reliable signals were the virtual table slot, the vtable a constructor stores, and callers confirmed by byte search; strings and imports helped nowhere in this batch.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions from the ped task region, with a confidence for each. The batch covers death and injury tasks, melee tasks with many small helpers, fall and get-up tasks, seek and follow tasks, and a factory plus a family of NaturalMotion task constructors.

What was found

Verified Joining every earlier naming lane against the inventory gives a near-unanimous slot table: slot 1 is clone, slot 3 returns the constant task id, slot 5 is make abortable, simple slot 17 is per-tick processing, and complex slots 18, 19 and 20 are create next, create first and control subtask. Slot 6 returns a float urgency. Slot 7 has two shapes at one slot: movement tasks copy a target point to the caller, while death and scenario tasks allocate a dummy task object.

Verified Constructors identify themselves twice: they store their class vtable after calling the base constructor, and the stored vtable can be read back through the symbol tables to confirm the class. This named over twenty constructors and destructors, including a full family of NaturalMotion ctors sharing one abstract base.

Verified Several follow and fall tasks build subtasks through small by-id factory helpers that switch on a task id constant, and one such helper was inventoried with size zero while being a real function.

Inferred The melee task keeps its state in three flag bytes tested by a family of one-bit getters, with neighbouring values identifying the move and action-result subtask ids. One id constant could not be read because its stub sits in the encrypted range, so that id stays inferred from usage.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep the majority slot wording: get task id over get task type, and per-class names at slots 6 and 7 where behaviour genuinely differs.
  • Resolve a constructor's class by reading its stored vtable back through the symbols instead of trusting caller context alone.
  • Confirm every relied-upon caller by searching for its call bytes and resolving the true containing function; nearest-inventory attribution is frequently wrong in dense unnamed regions.
  • Treat shared tiny symbols with suspicion: one widely referenced helper labelled as a script native is the global delete operator, and two verified rewrites carry guess names that vtable readback overturns.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble through the mapped image and check the mapping against a known function first. Gather per-function calls, string references and import calls into one table, then join prior lanes against the inventory to build the slot map. For constructors, read the stored vtable and resolve its first entries. For unclear helpers, scan the code section for call bytes targeting them, verify each site reads as a real call, and attribute it through the full function inventory rather than the nearest named entry.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified One create-first function is only a few bytes long but carries an inventory size that runs into its neighbour, so linear disassembly attributed the neighbour's calls to it. Byte search contradicted the listing and the raw bytes settled it.

Verified One inventory entry spans two manager thunks plus the start of an already verified function; it was named for the thunk at its start address.

Verified The first megabyte of code is encrypted on disk, so base-class virtuals and a few stubs decode as garbage. Nothing in the batch depended on them except one task id, which was inferred instead.

entry.title: Production batch: three ui rewrites verified, one float case the checker cannot settle
entry.summary: Three input-ui functions were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent over a thousand trials each, and a fourth was proven halfway; the interesting result is a single input pair where the checker's original side deterministically disagrees with three independent IEEE computations, so that pair stays excluded until a real x86 machine can adjudicate it.
entry.content:
Three input-ui functions were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent over a thousand trials each, and a fourth was proven halfway; the interesting result is a single input pair where the checker's original side deterministically disagrees with three independent IEEE computations, so that pair stays excluded until a real x86 machine can adjudicate it.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring input-ui functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original through the project's differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, written memory, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified A brightness-update function rounds through a magic-constant sequence (scale, add and subtract a large power of two, then a sign-dependent correction). With one input pair the scaled value lands exactly on a whole number, and there the original side answers one higher than every IEEE computation: exact rational arithmetic, correctly-rounded emulation, and an intrinsic-by-intrinsic replication of the same instruction sequence run on the same machine all agree with the rewrite. The split is stable across repeated identical trials, and a sweep of neighbouring inputs agrees everywhere except that exact point.

Verified The usual suspects were cleared one by one: the comparison instruction itself behaves correctly on zeros in a micro-test, both sides run with the default control word, and a second exact landing elsewhere does not diverge. The mechanism is still unknown, and it is contradiction-shaped: same emulator, same control word, same instructions, different answer.

Verified In the largest batch function, a color-helper call after two ordered float comparisons is dead code: the first test passes only if the blend exceeds the lookup, the second only if the lookup exceeds the blend, which cannot both hold. The contract leaves that call unpatched and relies on the checker's undeclared-write detection to shout if the analysis is ever wrong.

Verified A gate helper that two call sites invoke with no register setup takes no arguments; treating it as taking the leftover register value fails because the interception stub clobbers it. Checking sibling call sites settled the convention.

What was decided or recommended

  • The rewrite is IEEE-correct, so the single diverging input pair is excluded from the contract and recorded as narrowing, with a same-path replacement pair covering the same branch. A real-x86 re-run should restore the excluded pair first.
  • Lanes writing float-steering inputs should keep scaled values away from exact integers unless they are specifically testing the rounding boundary, and should verify per-trial paths rather than branch-shape counts, because distinct paths can share one call shape.
  • The half-proven large function continues from a staged retry kit: the passing entry stage plus a step-by-step plan for its loops and indirect calls.

How to reproduce it

Steer any rounding-magic sequence to an exact-integer landing with a zero residual and compare the worker's original side against a correctly-rounded emulation of the same operations; sweep the steering input across the boundary to confirm the divergence is confined to the exact point. The lane's scratch folder holds the sweep and stability scripts, the intrinsic replication probe, and the staged retry kit.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first probes failed on two unforced errors: hand-computed global addresses with a wrong high digit, and a two-argument call with the arguments swapped (the last value pushed is the first argument). Both are now machine-checked habits: addresses come from a script, and every multi-argument call is verified against push order. The deeper confusion was a frame-slot mis-trace that made a live code path look dead and a dead one look live; recomputing the stack pointer at every frame reference fixed it, and the corrected reading is what proved the color-helper path genuinely dead.

entry.title: Naming ped movement, blend and frag functions
entry.summary: One hundred seventeen of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and the batch exposed a slot-label trap every future naming lane should know: for move-task classes with two virtual tables, the same slot label names two different functions.
entry.content:
One hundred seventeen of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names, and the batch exposed a slot-label trap every future naming lane should know: for move-task classes with two virtual tables, the same slot label names two different functions.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, mostly from ped movement tasks, the on-foot movement blender, fragment physics instances and injury and death tasks. Only names, no rewrites.

What was found

Verified Move-task classes with two virtual tables reuse the same slot label in the inventory for a primary-table slot and a secondary-table slot. A prior lane correctly named the primary slot as clone while this batch held the secondary slot, a float setter, under the identical label. Slot numbers alone cannot name these classes.

Verified The ninth virtual slot of move tasks sets the target point, copying a position plus flags and, in one class, forwarding the update to its movement subtask after a task-type check. The fourth slot of the timed go-to-point task debits elapsed time when its subtask is unfinished.

Verified The movement blender's table base, a factory that builds the player on-foot task, its constructor and base destructor, and the feedback-interface constructor and destructors were all resolved by reading virtual tables and constructor call chains.

Verified Recurring families were named once and applied to each member: phase blend weights, blend slot id remapping, fragment subtree masking, per-type registry setup, attach-state updates, and four byte-identical feedback dispatchers that differ only in which virtual they call.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the established project slot conventions for task cloning and subtask phases, extended with target-point setting for slot nine. Thirty-three functions were left unnamed with the reason recorded, most of them bare getters to unlabeled fields or gated forwards to unknown base operations. The next naming lane in physics or animation should disassemble before trusting any slot label on a multiple-inheritance class, and should resolve constructor tables first since one table read names several functions.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the mapped executable image, collect its direct calls, imported calls and referenced strings into one table, resolve callee names against the merged project symbols and prior lane names, scan the code section for exact callers of unnamed functions, and read virtual-table slots to tie constructors and destructors to their classes. Short functions were read in full and large ones skimmed by call list and structure.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two inventory sizes were wrong: one clone overruns into its neighbour and two functions were listed with size zero, so reads had to be checked against padding bytes. Peeking at arbitrary mid-function offsets produced garbage disassembly twice before all reads were re-anchored to function entries. A few caller attributions resolve to a named function that merely precedes the true unnamed caller, and those are marked approximate in the report.

entry.title: Naming the movement-task function group
entry.summary: One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive movement-task functions received descriptive names, most at high confidence, by combining the project's inventory labels with vtable and caller evidence.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive movement-task functions received descriptive names, most at high confidence, by combining the project's inventory labels with vtable and caller evidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each function in a batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, which turned out to be almost entirely the pedestrian movement-task code: go-to-point, route following, wandering, formation, crowd, and related task classes.

What was found

Verified The task virtual-table slots have stable meanings across classes: slot one clones, slot three returns the task id constant, slot five makes the task abortable, and slots eighteen through twenty manage subtasks (create first, create next, control).

Verified Movement tasks carry a second thirteen-slot interface table whose slots the inventory labels do not distinguish from primary slots. Its slot seven copies the target point to an out-param, slot eight reads a per-task float with a slot-ten setter, and slot six holds per-class readiness checks. Every batch entry in these slots was assigned to the correct table by comparing table base addresses.

Verified Simple movement tasks run their per-tick update through slot twenty, which calls slots twenty-two and twenty-three to refresh speed and heading; the slot-seventeen process wrapper calls slot twenty first. One code stub is shared by address between a movement task and several UI layout classes through duplicate folding, with unrelated meanings on each side.

Verified Sixteen functions are non-virtual helpers. Caller analysis attributed twelve to a single owning class, mostly subtask factories used only by one task's create-first, create-next, and control methods.

Inferred The secondary slot-eight float behaves like a per-task arrival radius, with tight values for cover movement, loose values for road crossing, and a unit default for tracking, but no direct consumer was observed.

Unknown One area-search predicate matching model category three could not be named because the meaning of that model category is not established.

What was decided or recommended

  • Named one hundred twenty functions at high confidence from slot contracts, verified rewrites, and vtable proof, and twenty-nine at medium from fully read behaviour with project-style wording.
  • Future naming lanes over movement classes should verify the vtable base address for slots six through eight instead of trusting the slot label alone, since primary and secondary slots share numbering.
  • Caller attribution by nearest symbol should be treated as a hint only; two helpers in this batch belonged to unnamed functions immediately after the attributed one.

How to reproduce it

Re-run the lane's evidence gatherer (disassembly plus string, import, and named-callee collection for every batch function), the vtable scan (pointer scan of read-only data validated against runtime type records), and the whole-text caller scan from the lane scratch folder, then compare each function's slot and callers against the contracts above.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first version of the vtable scan found nothing because type descriptors live in writable data rather than read-only data, and because the type-name prefix contains a literal question mark the matching pattern dropped. Both were fixed and the scan then confirmed one hundred thirty-four functions with no mismatches. Two script-native labels on facing helpers look wrong (vector arguments, float results) and were treated as math helpers instead.
