entry.title: Seven verified rewrites compared a call's answer the wrong way, and how the last two were found
entry.summary: By the end of 5 October seven verified rewrites outside the leaderboard family had been withdrawn for one and the same mistake. This entry puts the day's findings in one place: what the mistake is, how often it occurs, how it was found from two directions, and what "verified" is worth in the light of it.
entry.content:
By the end of 5 October seven verified rewrites outside the leaderboard family had been withdrawn for one and the same mistake. This entry puts the day's findings in one place: what the mistake is, how often it occurs, how it was found from two directions, and what "verified" is worth in the light of it.

The mistake

The original calls something, compares the value that comes back, and branches with a signed conditional jump. The rewrite holds the returned value in an unsigned word, because that is what the checker's call macros and a plain function pointer give it, and compares it with an ordering operator. In Rust that comparison is unsigned. The two agree for every answer below two to the thirty-first and disagree for every answer with the high bit set. Contracts script a callee's answers by hand, and by hand people script small numbers.

MeasureValueStatus
Verified rewrites that compare a callee's answer with an ordering operator, found from the rewrites' text241Verified (audit lane's scan; a lower bound by design)
Of those measured, proofs that pass with the comparison's signedness flipped52 of 117Verified (two lanes, each function's own contract on the stock checker)
Of those measured, proofs that pass with the bound moved by one56 of 146Verified
Blind proofs read against the originalAbout 75; five rewrites wrongVerified; each wrong one read again by the coordinator before withdrawal
Verified functions whose original compares a call's returned value and follows it with a signed jump, found from the original's code570Verified (coordinator's sweep over every verified function)
Of those, flagged by a coarse count of signed comparisons in the rewriteSeven; two wrong, three right, two needing a closer readingVerified by reading
How good the coarse count isRun on the five rewrites withdrawn earlier, as they were, it catches fourVerified
Proofs made under older checker versions that the current one accepts unchanged178 of 180, none vacuousVerified (separate audit the same day)

Two directions

The audit started from the rewrites: find comparisons whose operand came from a call macro, build the wrong versions, run them through the existing contract. That measures the proofs, and it is how blindness was shown to be common. But its population is defined by what a text scan recognises, and it said so: calls made through a function pointer taken from an object's table are not call macros.

The sweep starts from the original: disassemble every verified function, and after each call look a few instructions ahead for a compare on the returned register, or a register it was copied to, followed by a signed jump, set or conditional move. That needs no checker run and takes thirteen seconds for the whole verified tree. Its population does not depend on how the rewrite spells a call. The two rewrites it found make virtual calls; neither was among the 241.

What this says about the count

  • The mistake is real and rare: seven found among roughly 15,800 verified functions, in a population of a few hundred functions where it can occur at all. The estimate will firm up when a lane has read all 570 sites exactly; the coarse count is known to miss cases.
  • A blind proof is usually a weak proof of a right rewrite: about nine in ten of the blind ones read so far were right. But "usually" is what the checker exists to replace.
  • The age of a proof is not the problem. Proofs made under the first four checker versions pass the sixth unchanged. The problem is a kind of input the method leaves to the lane's imagination: what a callee answers.
  • Every withdrawn rewrite returns only with a contract that scripts the boundary, its neighbours and values with the high bit set, and with a wrong version that is exactly this mistake and must fail. The production brief has required that for new work since the first case.

Decisions

  • All seven are withdrawn; strengthening lanes have repaired and re-proven the first and are working on the rest.
  • A lane is reading all 570 signed sites against their rewrites, site by site, and reporting every disagreement with the earlier hand adjudications.
  • The population at risk is defined from the original's code from now on, not from the rewrites' text.

How it ended (added at 23:00 the same day)

The lane read all 627 signed sites in the 570 functions against their rewrites: 622 right, four different, one an artefact of a function boundary in the inventory. Its verdicts agree with every earlier hand adjudication by four other lanes. Two of the four were new and were withdrawn, which brought the withdrawals for this pattern to nine.

One of the nine was withdrawn in error and has been restored. Its comparison is written unsigned where the original is signed, as the coordinator read it, but for every answer with the high bit set both branches of the original arrive at the same block: the repair lane ran a signed and an unsigned version against the original on 1,200 mixed trials and 600 more with every answer high-bit, and they agree, while a version with the bound moved by one fails. The coordinator had read the comparison and not followed the branches. So the count is eight observably wrong rewrites, not nine; this corrects the heading above and the two changelog entries that say seven and nine.

Six of the eight are repaired, re-proven with contracts that script boundary and high-bit answers and a wrong version with the flipped comparison that fails, and back in the verified tree. Two are still with a strengthening lane.

A limit found the same evening: the checker runs under an emulator

The development machine is an ARM laptop, and the original game is 32-bit x86, so every proof in this project runs the original and the rewrite under the operating system's x86 emulator. The pipeline's runners are real x86 machines. A differential test of a lifted function passed on the laptop and failed in the pipeline on one input: a signalling not-a-number handed back as a 64-bit value on the float stack. A real processor quiets it on the load; the emulator did not. Verified: one case, reproduced on every pipeline run until the test was changed to treat two not-a-numbers as equal, which is what the lift method says.

What follows from it is Inferred, not measured: where the emulator's float stack differs from a real processor's, a proof made here says that the rewrite matches the original as the emulator runs it. Both sides run under the same emulator, so most differences cancel; one that would not is a rewrite that moves a value through the float stack where the original moves it through integer registers, or the reverse. Nothing is known to be wrong because of this. It is the largest assumption under the word "verified" that has not been tested, and testing it needs the checker run on a real x86 machine with the owner's copy of the game.

To reproduce the sweep: for each verified function, disassemble the original, and for each call scan forward to the next call or return for a compare on the returned register followed by a signed conditional instruction; compare the count with the signed comparisons in the rewrite.

entry.title: Finishing a large staged function: shared slots with two arities
entry.summary: A large viewer method left half-proven by an earlier attempt was carried to full verification in five stages with one rewrite. The surprises were all in the calling shapes: one slot called with two different argument counts, an entry spill that changes which object the tail compares, and a loop index that resets on exhaustion.
entry.content:
A large viewer method left half-proven by an earlier attempt was carried to full verification in five stages with one rewrite. The surprises were all in the calling shapes: one slot called with two different argument counts, an entry spill that changes which object the tail compares, and a loop index that resets on exhaustion.

What was asked

Continue the staged proof of a large function deferred as partly proven in stages: two stages already passed, two planned. Finish the remaining stages so that one rewrite passes every stage contract and the stages together reach every branch and every callee.

What was found

  • Verified One rewrite now passes four stage contracts at one thousand trials each with zero failures, bit-exact floating point, and a caught deliberately-broken version per stage. A fifth diagnostic pass proved each of eight gate-fail trials fails at exactly its gate.
  • Verified Two indirect-call slots are each invoked once with no stack arguments and once with one stack word. Stack-balance analysis shows the pushed word belongs to the following call, which takes a value-plus-flag pair; the rewrite pushes both words there with identical logged arguments and final stack pointer, confirmed by the passing runs.
  • Verified The entry code spills an object pointer over its own incoming argument slot, so the tail compares that object rather than the entry argument. The spill sits below the checker's observed stack window, and the first probe caught the misreading immediately because the original called through the wrong table.
  • Verified A count-driven search loop keeps its trip index only when it finds a match and resets it to zero when the count runs out; the probe caught the first rewrite returning the exhausted count instead.
  • Verified In contract global values, per-trial rotation needs an explicit rotation entry; a bare list of values does not rotate and silently holds its first element on every trial. The symptom was two callees that never fired because one trial type never materialised.

What was decided or recommended

The function counts as verified: every branch and every callee is reached across the stages with no narrowed comparison. The gate-diagnostic pattern (one mutant per gate, each allowed to fail only on its own trial types) is a cheap way to prove fail-edge coverage when several edges share one tail; it is worth reusing on the next staged function with shared tails.

How to reproduce it

Each stage has a machine-written contract: scripted per-call answers, fabricated heap objects with planted indirect-call targets, and pinned inputs forcing each path in turn. The checker runs original and rewrite from identical state over one thousand trials per stage and compares memory writes, stack use, outgoing calls and faults. Deliberately broken rewrites confirmed each stage catches real differences, including one caught by a single heap byte.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first stage probe faulted in the original before any new code ran, because the cascade object had been misread as the entry argument instead of the spilled object. A later probe failed only on exhaust trials, which exposed the index reset. A third showed zero failures yet was judged vacuous, which exposed the non-rotating global list. All three were contract or rewrite bugs, fixed without touching the checker.

entry.title: How many old proofs would the current checker accept
entry.summary: Asked. Proofs accepted under checker versions 1-4 predate version 3's vacuity marking and later tightenings. What share of them would the current version-6 checker still accept as they stand, and does that share differ by checker version or by kind of function?
entry.content:
Asked. Proofs accepted under checker versions 1-4 predate version 3's vacuity marking and later tightenings. What share of them would the current version-6 checker still accept as they stand, and does that share differ by checker version or by kind of function?

Method (Verified). A random sample of 180 verified functions with version 1-4 proofs was re-run through its own unchanged contracts (only the rewrite DLL path repointed) on the stock version-6 worker. FINDINGS-TBD.

What was found (Verified). RESULTS-TBD.

Two failures, both checker-side (Verified). One proof fails because both sides make more calls than the default call-log cap on a few trials; the two sides agree exactly, but the checker fails truncated trials. The other fails on a single trial where the function computes a data address that lands in executable code pages: the original reads it without remark, while the rewrite side faults because the checker revokes code pages while the rewrite runs. In both cases the rewrite mirrors the original; the check, not the rewrite, rejects the proof.

Decided. Nothing repaired (measurement lane). The two failing proofs need contract-level handling: a raised call-log cap for the first, narrowed inputs that keep computed reads out of code pages for the second. Vacuous proofs need contracts whose declared callees actually fire (details in the lane report).

Reproduce. Lane folder k-vac under the scratch area: manifest.json (sample + staged contracts), results.json (per-function class), analysis.json (shares with confidence intervals), report.md (full findings).

entry.title: Naming a batch of scanner, task, camera and cutscene functions
entry.summary: One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive functions were named, with the strongest new signal being that the last simple-task virtual slot is the attack method, confirmed by its only three overrides.
entry.content:
One hundred forty-nine of one hundred fifty consecutive functions were named, with the strongest new signal being that the last simple-task virtual slot is the attack method, confirmed by its only three overrides.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name and no rewriting.

What was found

  • Verified The batch splits into four clusters: entity scanners with one assess worker per ped event family, destroy-car and driveby task virtuals with their helpers, cutscene camera slot management with the animation player, and the cutscene object with draw emission, probe lighting and bounds.
  • Verified Joining several thousand vtable entries from earlier batches against the names other lanes gave confirms the task slot vocabulary: clone, task id, abort handler, per-frame processing, and first, next and control subtask methods, each agreed by dozens of prior names.
  • Verified The last simple-task virtual slot is the attack method: only three overrides exist in plain code, belonging to the fire-gun, melee-result and gang-driveby tasks, and each one calls attack routines. This sets the naming convention for that slot.
  • Verified Three tiny routines that only appear as pushed constants are animation-end callbacks, installed through one shared installer routine alongside a flag and a context pointer, each marking its own task finished.
  • Verified Six near-identical function pairs differ only in parameters such as a table word, an argument count, a track tag or a probe selector; byte-diffing each pair before naming kept them distinct.
  • Inferred Several low-confidence merged symbol labels look wrong: two encrypted stubs behave as the new and delete operators, one ubiquitous call is the event-submit helper rather than a helmet native, and the supposed task-only allocator is used by animation and cutscene constructors too.

What was decided or recommended

Forty-nine names were recorded at high confidence from slot plus shape, one hundred at medium from close reading, and one function was left empty at low confidence because its callee is unidentified. Later lanes should reuse the slot-join approach for task batches, byte-diff twin functions before naming them, and treat the low-confidence merged labels above with suspicion.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per function with direct-call targets resolved against verified rewrites and lane names, imports, string references and constant returns; scan the code section once for callers of every batch function; read the short functions and the unclear ones fully; join vtable evidence from all earlier naming batches against lane names to derive slot meanings; byte-diff near-identical neighbours.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first evidence pass indexed the memory-mapped image by file offset instead of by address offset and decoded padding as code; decoding one known tiny function end to end exposed the mistake immediately. Two caller names used as supporting evidence appear mislabeled, so every name in this batch rests on the function's own body rather than on its callers.

entry.title: How many proofs are blind to a flipped comparison: a measurement
entry.summary: About four in ten verified proofs covering a comparison on a callee's answer cannot see that comparison's signedness being flipped, and about one in three cannot see its bound moved by one. Five spot-checks against the original found the rewrites right and only the proofs weak, but the sample is small and hand-picked.
entry.content:
About four in ten verified proofs covering a comparison on a callee's answer cannot see that comparison's signedness being flipped, and about one in three cannot see its bound moved by one. Five spot-checks against the original found the rewrites right and only the proofs weak, but the sample is small and hand-picked.

What was asked

After over a hundred verified rewrites were withdrawn because they compared a length unsigned where the original compares signed, the project needed a measurement: how many verified proofs are blind to a signedness change or an off-by-one bound on a value returned by a callee. The plan was to find such comparisons by script, build two one-change wrong versions per sampled function (other signedness, bound moved by one), run each through the function's existing contract unchanged, and count how many pass.

What was found

Verified A scripted scan found 241 verified rewrites (about three percent of the verified tree, excluding one template family handled separately) that compare a callee-returned value with an ordering comparison, directly or through one local. Sixty were sampled with a fixed seed, spread across lane kinds and sizes; 57 validated (three excluded when their correct version came back vacuous under the current driver).

Verified Of the validated functions, 20 of 45 sign-flipped wrong versions passed (44 percent, 95 percent interval 31 to 59), and 20 of 57 bound-shifted wrong versions passed (35 percent, interval 24 to 48). That implies roughly 107 sign-blind and 85 bound-blind proofs in the 241. Thirty-two of the 57 functions were blind to at least one of the two changes. Every failing wrong version failed on genuine trial differences, and the blindness was spread across lane kinds and function sizes rather than confined to one group.

Verified Five blind cases were checked against the original by reading the comparison the original actually makes. All five rewrites were right; the proofs were merely weak because the contracts never answer the callee with the values that would distinguish the mutants (a negative answer, a zero, the exact boundary).

Inferred The cause is structural, as suspected: a value a function receives directly is generated with edge cases, while a callee's answer is whatever the lane scripted, and lanes script small values that steer down the function's paths. One lane's own notes even record that its trials cover only the negative path.

What was decided or recommended

The 32 blind functions are listed in the lane's data files with the exact comparison and which wrong version passed, so re-run lanes can strengthen exactly those contracts. The recommended strengthening is to script the callee answer at the comparison boundary, one above and below it, and one large or negative value, then re-run both wrong versions and require both to fail. Extending the measurement to the full 150-function sample needs only more runs, and a random subset of the blind list still needs checking against the original.

How to reproduce it

From the repository: scan the verified rewrites for ordering comparisons whose operands resolve to callee-slot calls directly or through one local; draw the seeded stratified sample; build the sign-flip and bound-shift wrong versions with one text-level change each; assemble one proof crate holding the correct version plus both wrong versions per function; run each variant through the function's existing contract unchanged on the stock checker worker at the contract's own trial count; count passes. The lane's scratch folder holds the scripts, the sample, the per-function outcomes, and the blind list.

What was confusing or went wrong

The lane was stopped from outside midway and restarted; its scratch folder held everything, so the rerun lost no work. On resume, the first collection round reported all 60 correct runs failing, which turned out to be the collector reading the wrong verdict field rather than any real failure. Two resume-log timestamps were written from memory about fifteen minutes fast and had to be corrected from the machine clock. Two tracked verified files were found truncated or dangling, and six needed helpers from their lane's crate root, copied verbatim into the scratch crate.

entry.title: A full class batch verified, including a float returned on the x87 stack
entry.summary: A production lane verified all 42 animation-channel methods in its batch, and proved that a function returning a float on the x87 stack can be checked today with an f32 rewrite return and the x87 state comparison.
entry.content:
A production lane verified all 42 animation-channel methods in its batch, and proved that a function returning a float on the x87 stack can be checked today with an f32 rewrite return and the x87 state comparison.

What was asked

Rewrite 42 related animation-channel methods in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original, with 1,000 trials and a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All 42 methods passed 1,000 trials each with every wrong version caught; none were deferred.

Verified A Rust rewrite declared to return f32 leaves the value in the x87 ST0 register on this target, and the checker's x87 state comparison verifies it bit for bit, including signed zeros and quiet not-a-numbers. The brief lists x87 returns as not provable; that holds for doubles, but a single-precision x87 return works with no return channel compared and the x87 state check on.

Verified Indirect calls cannot be site-patched (the driver refuses anything that is not a direct call). They are intercepted by planting a stub address in the fabricated object table and having the rewrite load and call through it exactly like the original.

Verified Three separate copy and serialize loops return a reloaded count, not the last value they moved: each loop ends by loading the count into the return register after the final element. Two first attempts returned the last element and failed; reading the last register write before the return, not the loop body, gives the right answer.

What was decided or recommended

Lanes with an x87 single-precision return should attempt it with an f32 rewrite signature instead of deferring. Lanes should check what value the return register holds after a loop rather than assuming it holds the last computed value. The indirect-call planting pattern is now demonstrated and reusable.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker driver and worker; each verdict records 1,000 passing trials and each wrong-version verdict records a failure on the x87, heap, call or return comparison as appropriate.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two first attempts misread the original: a decoder slot was assumed to carry the object pointer when address arithmetic showed it carries the bit cursor, and a thread-block accessor was dereferenced once too often. A build briefly failed because a finished run still held the rewrite library file; a retry seconds later succeeded. All were fixed and re-proven in the same session.

entry.title: A stuck tick stopped the lanes: how one slow step took down three agents
entry.summary: At 18:40 on 5 October every lane the project was running stopped at once. Nothing had crashed. A chain of three ordinary things did it, and each link had looked safe on its own.
entry.content:
At 18:40 on 5 October every lane the project was running stopped at once. Nothing had crashed. A chain of three ordinary things did it, and each link had looked safe on its own.

LinkWhat happenedStatus
A finished lane left work runningA production lane ended at 17:54 and reported that nothing of its own was still running. Seventeen copies of one of its helper scripts were, and stayed busy for 52 to 117 minutes, about four processor cores between them. The watchdog stops such leftovers only when they are two and a half hours old.Verified (process list, command lines, ages)
The five-minute tick slowed to a crawlThe tick's rewrite importer reads every lane's results, about 1,500 folders, and normally takes a minute. From 18:30 it ran for more than ten, reading about 120 files a second with the disk idle and no paging. After the leftovers were stopped the same step took 57 seconds.Timing verified; the leftovers as the cause is inferred from that before and after, not proven
The supervisor waits for the tickThe supervisor starts lanes and runs the tick itself, and runs as one background task with a two-hour limit. It is written to finish by itself after 112 minutes. It was inside the tick when the 112 minutes passed, was still there when the two hours passed, and was stopped at the limit.Verified (supervisor log, task record)
Lanes are the supervisor's childrenStopping the task stopped everything it had started: three lanes that were 30 to 45 minutes into their work, among them the audit of blind proofs and the first class-completion lane.Verified

What was lost and what was not

No results were lost: lanes keep their state in their own folders and write results as they go. About two lane-hours of model work were interrupted, and for seven minutes nothing was running. A fourth lane had finished four minutes earlier and is unaffected: it verified 26 of 27 tiny forwarding functions in 25 minutes, all of them deferred as untestable by the project's earliest lanes, because the checker of that day could not follow a jump out of a function.

Changes

  • Every step of the tick has a time limit. A step that overruns is stopped with its whole process tree, the tick says so, and the remaining steps run. The limits add up to under fourteen minutes.
  • The supervisor runs no tick in the last eight minutes of its window, and the window is 100 minutes, so the worst case ends before the task's limit.
  • The lane launcher recognises a lane that was cut off from outside (its log shows a launch, work, and no exit) and resumes it from its folder instead of starting it again. The three lanes were resumed this way.
  • The watchdog stops a lane's leftover processes five minutes after that lane's launcher has logged its exit, instead of after two and a half hours.

What it says more generally

A lane's own statement that it left nothing running is a claim, not a fact; the check has to be made from outside, soon after the lane ends. And a controller that does housekeeping in its own loop inherits every way the housekeeping can stall.

entry.title: The largest families are the emptiest: what went into the workspace from the first two lifts, and what did not
entry.summary: Two lanes have now lifted families of verified functions into generic, portable Rust: the leaderboard class (3,195 verified rewrites) and four more families (2,392). The coordinator reviewed both trees today and moved two crates into the workspace. Three families were left out, and the reason changes how lift targets are chosen.
entry.content:
Two lanes have now lifted families of verified functions into generic, portable Rust: the leaderboard class (3,195 verified rewrites) and four more families (2,392). The coordinator reviewed both trees today and moved two crates into the workspace. Three families were left out, and the reason changes how lift targets are chosen.

FamilyVerified functions behind itWhat the lifted code holdsDecision
Leaderboard class: six table lookups, a probe, a row collector3,195Eight generic functions with loops, comparisons and a result map each, and one descriptor per leaderboard. Behaviour.In the workspace as crates/lf-leaderboard. Verified: 13 host tests pass; the pipeline built and tested it on Windows, Linux and macOS.
Script native handlers2,162Four short forwarding functions and a table: per native its name, its hash where known, how many script words it forwards, which of them are booleans, and how the answer is returned. Data, and useful data: it is the script machine's interface to the engine.In the workspace as crates/lf-script-natives, described as a dispatch table and not as lifted behaviour. Verified: 6 host tests pass.
Timer callback registrations81One function that makes one call through a trait, and a table of a name and an index per member. Most names are fragments of addresses, because nobody has named the things being registered. Nothing else.Not brought in and not counted as lifted. Each original passes one address to a registrar; the address is the whole content, and the lifted form replaces it with an index that means nothing yet. These are tables waiting for names.
Asset slot registrations80
Stored ratio refreshes69

Why it happened

The coordinator's brief for the second lift said to take the largest groups of same-shaped functions, in order of size. A group is large when the compiler stamped out one tiny routine hundreds of times, and the routines stamped out most often are start-up registrations and forwarders. So choosing by member count selects for the functions with the least in them. The lane did what it was asked, well, and its report said plainly where each crate's owner was unknown. The count it produced, "5,587 verified functions covered by lifted code", was true by its own definition and overstated what a port gains by at least those 230.

What a better target looks like

A class whose every method is verified: it has behaviour, it has a boundary the game itself drew, and nothing is missing in the middle. A census by class name (the part of a function's name before the last scope separator) gives, today:

MeasureValueStatus
Game functions with a class-qualified nameAbout 9,800 of 37,413Verified (census script over the inventory, the naming lanes and the verified index)
Classes with four or more named methods, all verified21 classes, 127 functions, 16,600 bytes, outside the leaderboard family: three audio voice classes, several animation channel decoders, a streaming device, a few task classesVerified
Classes with 70% or more of their bytes verified but not all467 classes, missing 1,327 functions and 60,000 bytes between themVerified
What "all verified" leaves outMethods nobody has named yet are invisible to the census. A class counted as complete may have virtual functions that are still anonymous.Known limit

Decisions

  • Lift targets are classes verified in full, not the largest shape groups. The animation channel decoders are first: 14 related classes, 100 named methods, 55 verified.
  • Production lanes take functions in address order, so a class is finished only by accident. A new kind of lane takes the missing methods of named classes, with the verified methods of the same classes named as the place to start. The first one has 42 methods of the animation channel classes.
  • A lifted function counts as lifted only if behaviour is in it. A family whose members differ only in an address is recorded as a table, and reported separately.
  • Both crates say in their own documentation that the lane's differential run against the verified rewrites has not been repeated by the pipeline. The test crates are large generated files and are still to come.

Follow-up on the 144 withdrawn rewrites

The entry "Verified, and wrong" recorded 144 rewrites of the leaderboard row collector that compared a length unsigned. A re-run lane has re-proven all 144 with the signed comparison. Its contracts script sixteen answers for the length helper, ten of them negative or edge values, and bias the other scripted answers so that those lengths reach the comparison; the unsigned mistake, run as a wrong version, fails on every one of the 144. They are back in the verified count. The same lane found the blind spot next door in the other direction: a neighbouring function of the family compares a count unsigned, its contracts script counts from 0 to 16 only, and a rewrite that compared signed would pass. That family and the 253 row-collector rewrites that were right but had the same blind proof are queued for the same treatment. Correction to the earlier entry: it gave the number of signed members as 269; by the verified index it is 253 with the family's standard name, plus a dozen named differently.

To reproduce the census: group the game's functions by the class part of their names and compare each group with the verified index.

entry.title: Float operand order needs a branch, not a black box
entry.summary: A production lane verifying audio functions found that the standard ways of pinning floating-point operand order do not work: the compiler swapped operands past both black-box barriers and opaque call boundaries, and only an explicit both-NaN branch pins the order by construction. Two functions were verified with the branch design; a third is deferred with a complete plan.
entry.content:
A production lane verifying audio functions found that the standard ways of pinning floating-point operand order do not work: the compiler swapped operands past both black-box barriers and opaque call boundaries, and only an explicit both-NaN branch pins the order by construction. Two functions were verified with the branch design; a third is deferred with a complete plan.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighbouring audio functions in Rust and prove each rewrite bit-identical to the original with the checker, including bit-exact floating-point results with matching NaN signs. Two were verified over 1200 trials each with mutants caught; the third was fully triaged and deferred for time with an executable plan.

What was found

  • Verified The compiler swaps the operands of scalar float add and multiply even when the values pass through black-box barriers and even across no-inline call boundaries. Both swaps were seen in disassembly of built rewrites. Order decides the sign of a NaN result, so a swapped build fails trials that pair two differently-signed NaNs in one operation.
  • Verified Order matters only when both operands are NaN: a single NaN forwards that NaN either way, and invalid cases yield the same default NaN either way. Both shipped rewrites therefore test the bit patterns first, forward the destination operand explicitly on both-NaN, and run a plain operation otherwise. Subtraction and comparisons need no branch.
  • Verified A build that had silently swapped an addition still passed small probes, purely because no trial paired two NaNs there. The lesson is that float contracts must include both-NaN pairs with opposing signs in the same operation, or a luck-dependent proof looks full.
  • Verified The contract lint check caught two wrong patch offsets before anything ran, exactly the failure mode it exists to stop.

What was decided or recommended

  • Both rewrites in this batch use the NaN-branch design; one was retrofitted from the opaque-call form and re-verified, because the opaque-call form is rebuild-fragile.
  • Recommended: amend the brief's float rule so black box stays (it stops constant folding) but the order pin is the NaN branch, and require opposing-sign NaN pairs in float input pools.
  • Previously verified float rewrites that rely on the black box alone are correct as built, but a toolchain change could silently swap them; re-running their contracts after such a change would catch it.

How to reproduce it

Build any rewrite whose float helpers are plain operations wrapped only in black boxes, disassemble the helper, and check which parameter ends up as the instruction destination; then run trials pairing plus-NaN with minus-NaN in one addition. The lane's report records the exact trial shape (a sum of three products over infinite and NaN inputs) and a pool layout that keeps the call path hot while carrying NaN coverage.

What was confusing or went wrong

  • For several builds the lane believed a memory source operand propagates NaN signs differently from a register source. That theory was wrong: re-examination found a swapped addition missed in an interleaved listing. It cost about twenty minutes and is recorded so nobody chases it again.
  • One rebuild failed on a locked output file because a worker from the previous run was still exiting; waiting for prior processes to clear before rebuilding fixed it.
  • The deferred function hides two quirks future lanes should know: two of its three multi-argument call shapes pass identical arguments and differ only in one register, and that register carries uninitialized frame fill (zero) in two shapes. Both were verified by hand-tracking the stack pointer and are in the lane report.

entry.title: Pin cycles in lockstep hide branch combinations
entry.summary: Verified A contract whose pinned inputs all cycle with the same period tests far fewer branch combinations than its author thinks: equal-length cycles march in lockstep, so some flag pairs never co-occur. Giving each pin a different cycle length took one function from four to ten call shapes with no other change.
entry.content:
Verified A contract whose pinned inputs all cycle with the same period tests far fewer branch combinations than its author thinks: equal-length cycles march in lockstep, so some flag pairs never co-occur. Giving each pin a different cycle length took one function from four to ten call shapes with no other change.

What was asked

Rewrite and verify a single large audio function with eleven scripted callees and about ten flag-driven branches.

What was found

Verified The first passing run covered only four call shapes. Three flag pins with two values each always agreed with the main enable flag, so whole combinations (a shaper call after the worker call, a path without the final helper) never ran, and both self-initialising parameter blocks only ever took their already-initialised path.

Verified A related gap: scripted callee outputs are consumed only on trials where that callee fires, so some script rows are dead and live rows can miss values the real callee produces. One row meant to drive a negative-index path never coincided with its callee firing.

Verified After giving pins cycle lengths of two, three, four, five and six, and placing script rows on live phases, the same rewrite passed with ten call shapes, every callee firing hundreds of times, and every parameter-block path taken.

What was decided or recommended

Pin cycles in a contract should use differing lengths so flag combinations mix across trials, and script rows for conditionally fired callees should be audited for which trial phases actually consume them. Both checks are cheap and static.

How to reproduce it

Take any contract with two or more equal-length pin cycles on branch flags, run it, and count distinct call shapes in the verdict coverage. Then change one cycle length and re-run: new shapes appear.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first deliberately wrong version of the rewrite passed all trials: the omitted store wrote back the value just read on some paths and was overwritten by a scripted callee output on the rest. It was replaced with a wrong version that omits a store nothing masks, which fails on the heap comparison as required.

entry.title: Two audio updates verified, and two disassembly traps
entry.summary: Both functions in this audio batch now have verified Rust rewrites, each proved identical to the original over 1200 trials, but the interesting part of the lane was the two mistakes in reading the original that the checker caught.
entry.content:
Both functions in this audio batch now have verified Rust rewrites, each proved identical to the original over 1200 trials, but the interesting part of the lane was the two mistakes in reading the original that the checker caught.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring audio-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the project checker, including a deliberately wrong version per function that the proof must reject.

What was found

Verified Both rewrites passed all 1200 trials with bit-exact float comparison, all checks on, and each wrong version was rejected for the right reason.

Verified A pushed register before a call is an argument, not a save. One function pushes a register and then its actual argument before calling a filter; reading the first push as a register save understates the callee's arity by one, which shifts every later stack read by four bytes. The same filter is called elsewhere with two visible pushes and no caller cleanup, which proves it pops two words.

Verified A flag-capture followed by a test and a conditional jump tests the test, not the capture. The sequence captures the floating-point comparison flags into a byte register, masks that byte, and jumps on parity — but the masking instruction itself overwrites the flags first, so the jump observes the parity of the masked value. The result is equality against a constant, not the NaN check it resembles: only an exactly equal input takes one side.

Verified Speed-reading drops instructions. Three one-line register reloads were missed on the first pass, each of which changed a call argument or a branch on some path. A mechanical listing of every write to the register found all three at once.

What was decided or recommended

Count pushes against caller cleanup to fix callee arity, and cross-check the same callee at its other call sites before writing the contract. Audit every stack-slot read against the pushes outstanding at that exact point, and grep for register writes rather than trusting a first read.

How to reproduce it

Run the two contracts in the lane folder with the stock checker driver and worker; each passes 1200 trials with bit-exact floats, and each bundled wrong version fails. The contract generators, the per-trial diagnosis script, and the full report with evidence labels are in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

The parity-trap finding took the longest: the wrong mental model predicted one constant on a trial where the original wrote zero, and every theory about scripting or indexing failed until the flag flow was re-read instruction by instruction. The pushed-register finding went through a longer loop first, including a stretch suspecting the checker's stub code of clobbering a register it provably preserves, before the missed reloads explained everything.

entry.title: Cmpnless means greater-than
entry.summary: A large blend routine failed its proof on exact-integer loop counts only, because the disassembler's cmpnless mnemonic was transcribed as not-less-than when it is predicate 6, not-less-or-equal, a greater-than test.
entry.content:
A large blend routine failed its proof on exact-integer loop counts only, because the disassembler's cmpnless mnemonic was transcribed as not-less-than when it is predicate 6, not-less-or-equal, a greater-than test.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring routines of one animation subsystem in Rust and prove each identical to the original over a thousand trials.

What was found

Verified All four routines verified with bit-exact floating point results and a caught wrong version each; the largest is proven on its main path with the remaining paths specified as a retry kit.

Verified The blend routine counts loop iterations with a round-and-fixup idiom whose final test disassembles as cmpnless. That mnemonic is comparison predicate 6, which is true when the first operand is greater than the second, not when it is not less than it. The two readings differ only when both operands are equal, so every fractional quotient rounded correctly and only exact integers miscounted: the original ran three iterations where the rewrite ran two. A probe contract that added exactly one to an output per iteration measured both counts directly and confirmed the one-line fix.

Inferred The checker's call stand-in zeroes the upper words of one vector register on the original side between two neighbouring helper calls. Only unlogged registers are affected, so no verdict is at risk, but one helper's vector argument had to stay uncompared because of it.

What was decided or recommended

Transcribe cmpnless as greater-than everywhere; audit other rewrites that read it as not-less-than, since the bug hides on all non-integer inputs. Anyone extending the blend proof should start from the retry kit in the lane report.

How to reproduce it

Pin the routine's two vector inputs and the limit it reads from its object so the quotient is an exact integer, stub the helpers with fixed rows, and compare iteration counts; or read predicate 6 in the processor manual's compare-pages.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first mismatch looked like a broken formula: every output word differed. Pinning each path separately showed the tail and the loop-free paths passing, which isolated the loop; only then did a counting probe reveal a miscount rather than a miscomputation. Two earlier hypotheses, relocated float constants and mismatched stub rows, were each disproven by a direct check before the instruction reading was questioned.

entry.title: Lifting the next families: script natives and three more
entry.summary: Four tiny routines now cover 2,392 verified functions: nearly every script native handler is one dispatch routine in four return conventions, and the timer, asset-slot and ratio-refresh groups are one routine each. Every member is proven against its verified rewrite by differential test.
entry.content:
Four tiny routines now cover 2,392 verified functions: nearly every script native handler is one dispatch routine in four return conventions, and the timer, asset-slot and ratio-refresh groups are one routine each. Every member is proven against its verified rewrite by differential test.

What was asked

Repeat the leaderboard lift on the next largest families of verified functions: script native handlers in several shapes, timer register callbacks, asset slot getters and refresh ratio writers, taking them one proven group at a time.

What was found

Verified The native handlers are far more uniform than their count suggests. Of 2,620 verified handlers, 2,162 are one engine call forwarding sequential script words, with per-word boolean coercion and four return conventions: return the answer, store its low byte, store the whole word, or return zero. What varies per handler is only its dispatch entry: name, hash, word count and coercion flags.

Verified The other three groups are each exactly one routine: timer callbacks pass one address to a registrar, asset slots pass a slot record and a name to a registry routine, and ratio refreshers divide two stored floats into a third. All 80 asset names were read back from the executable and match.

Verified The census corrected two labels from the earlier survey: the second native group forwards two arguments with no return, and most timer-group members carry other names. Operand-level checking also surfaced real variants the structural hash had merged: boolean coercions, a stack-slot quirk word, float-answering engine calls, and zero returns.

FamilyMembers proven

Timer registrations81
Asset registrations80
Ratio refreshes69

What was decided or recommended

  • Natives go to the script subsystem, timer registrations to the main loop; asset slots probably belong to streaming and the ratio bank's owner is still unknown, so it keeps its own crate for now.
  • 458 natives are deferred with stated reasons: bespoke argument plumbing, global-gated handlers that need their subsystem state first, float-computing handlers that form their own group, and spellings that need their lane's context layout.
  • Next groups in order: model registrations, timer initialisers, vehicle ratios, leaderboard constructors, and cache lookups.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's census and generator scripts over the verified rewrites to rebuild the descriptor tables and differential cases, then run the seven differential suites on the 32-bit target and the four crates' own tests on the 64-bit host. Every case also runs a deliberately wrong lift that must be caught. Together with the leaderboard family, 5,587 verified rewrites are now covered by lifted code.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Three defects were found by the proof rather than by reading: engine calls declared with float answers read a different return register than integer stubs provide, so those cases needed float-answering stubs; a residue spelling in store returns needed pinning per member instead of assuming two spellings; and parallel test suites shared one relocated base until each suite took it inside its own session. Each fix was confirmed by the full suite going green.
